author: Dr. Charles Dorner

slides.title: The audience changes while the producer stays useful
keyPoints: A feed receives readings from 0 through 100
Independent views ask to receive events
Closed views must not leave callable dead objects
slides.narration: A feed receives a reading of four. A total display needs it now, and a log or alert view may need the next reading too. Those views can open and close independently. Hard-coding every view into the feed makes the producer change whenever its audience changes. Polling can also be a poor fit when every event matters. Observer gives interested objects a way to register for updates through a shared contract. That solves the connection problem, but it does not choose ownership, duplicate handling, or failure behavior for us. In this lecture we will treat those delivery rules as part of the design, not as details hidden behind a notify method.

question.prompt: What should adding a new listener type avoid changing?
question.answer: The producer’s knowledge of concrete listener classes. A new type should receive events through the existing update contract.

slides.title: Direct updates work for a fixed audience
keyPoints: Two known views can be ordinary local variables
Validate the input before either update
No registration machinery is needed for a fixed lifetime
slides.narration: Our baseline has one total and one latest-reading display represented by integers. The publish function checks the input range, then updates both by reference. This is a reasonable implementation when the audience is fixed and both values remain alive during every call. After readings four and three, the total is seven and the latest value is three. The code contains no subscription list because its requirement does not need one. The limitation appears when views become independent objects with separate lifetimes and different update behavior. At that point the feed should talk through a shared interface rather than acquire another named argument for every new screen component.

question.prompt: What output distinguishes an accumulating view from a latest-value view?
question.answer: The total prints seven after four and three; the latest-value view prints only three.

slides.title: Sending events is a contract, not just a loop
keyPoints: Decide duplicate registration behavior
Decide mutation and nested-delivery rules
Decide what callback failure leaves behind
slides.narration: Before selecting a smart pointer, write three event stories. The same view registers twice: does it receive one event or two? A callback opens another view: can the registration list change during traversal? A callback throws after changing its own state: do later listeners still run? The chapter answers one, no, and no. It suppresses duplicate live identities, rejects subscription mutation during publish, and stops on the first callback exception. These are deliberate choices, not rules imposed by the Observer name. Writing them first gives tests meaningful targets. A different event library may make different choices and still implement Observer correctly, provided its observable contract is clear.
actions: Collect predictions for the three event stories, then state the chapter policy.

question.prompt: Does the pattern name decide whether a throwing listener prevents later updates?
question.answer: No. Fail-fast or continue-and-collect are separate delivery policies that must be documented and tested.

slides.title: An exception does not undo earlier listener work
keyPoints: The first listener changes its state, then throws
Delivery stops before the second listener
Catching the error does not reverse the first addition
slides.narration: This short program models two registered actions using callable objects so we can focus on delivery order before lifetime machinery. The first action adds five to first and throws. The loop exits through the catch, so the second action never receives the event. The outputs are therefore first five and second zero. Both facts matter: the failing listener was not unchanged, and the later listener was not called. This is fail-fast delivery with partial effects. A catch block is not a rollback operation. The chapter's Total behaves similarly when its optional after hook throws, and Feed promises only to reset its temporary busy flag so another publication can begin later.

question.prompt: After catching the callback error, should first be zero because publish failed?
question.answer: No. The addition already happened. This delivery policy does not roll back listener state.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Accept readings from zero through one hundred.
Notify each registered live listener once in registration order.
Skip expired listeners; reject null registration, nested publish, and subscription changes during publish.
slides.narration:
A feed with explicit notification rules. Feed keeps weak registrations and locks each one for the duration of its call. A scope guard clears the in-progress flag on all exits. Callback errors stop delivery and propagate without claiming rollback.

Accept readings from zero through one hundred. Notify each registered live listener once in registration order. Skip expired listeners; reject null registration, nested publish, and subscription changes during publish.

Only a successfully locked listener receives update. Duplicate live registrations produce one call. Registration storage does not change while being traversed. notifying_ is cleared when a publish call exits, including by exception. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. Borrowed raw pointers can be lean when a strict external lifetime and unsubscribe protocol is enforced. A snapshot of strong pointers simplifies stable delivery but keeps listeners alive for the whole batch and changes removal semantics.

comparisons.label: Chosen design
comparisons.text: Feed keeps weak registrations and locks each one for the duration of its call. A scope guard clears the in-progress flag on all exits. Callback errors stop delivery and propagate without claiming rollback.

comparisons.label: A reasonable alternative
comparisons.text: Borrowed raw pointers can be lean when a strict external lifetime and unsubscribe protocol is enforced. A snapshot of strong pointers simplifies stable delivery but keeps listeners alive for the whole batch and changes removal semantics.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Observer implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Only a successfully locked listener receives update. Duplicate live registrations produce one call. Registration storage does not change while being traversed. notifying_ is cleared when a publish call exits, including by exception.

slides.title: The problem: several views need the same new reading
keyPoints: A data feed receives small integer readings between zero and one hundred.
We need a way for a view to ask for notifications and later disappear without leaving a callable pointer to a destroyed object.
slides.narration:
A data feed receives small integer readings between zero and one hundred. A total display needs each new reading; another view may later log values or raise a local alert. The simplest feed directly calls the known views. For a fixed pair that may be enough. The limitation appears when views open and close independently. Adding every view type to the feed couples data delivery to user-interface details, while repeatedly polling the feed can miss changes or waste work.

We need a way for a view to ask for notifications and later disappear without leaving a callable pointer to a destroyed object. A listener is an object that receives an update. A publisher sends updates to registered listeners. The Observer pattern connects these roles through a shared interface so the publisher knows how to notify, but does not need to know each view’s class. Choosing the interface is only the start; the more difficult work is deciding lifetime and behavior during notification.

question.prompt: A view disappears while a feed continues to exist. Should the feed's registration alone keep that view alive?
question.answer: This example says no. Registration expresses interest in updates, not permanent ownership. Delivery must check that a listener still exists and keep it alive only while invoking it.

slides.title: Separate registration from ownership
keyPoints: Listener declares virtual update(int), and Total implements it.
The statement if (auto live = weak.lock()) both creates the temporary pointer and tests whether it is nonempty.
slides.narration:
Listener declares virtual update(int), and Total implements it. Feed stores weak_ptr<Listener> values. A weak pointer observes an object managed by shared_ptr without keeping that object alive. main owns the live Total through shared_ptr; Feed owns only registration entries. Before calling a listener, publish uses weak.lock to obtain a temporary shared_ptr. A successful lock keeps that particular listener alive until the local live pointer is released. A failed lock means the listener has expired, so the feed skips it.

The statement if (auto live = weak.lock()) both creates the temporary pointer and tests whether it is nonempty. That C++ condition keeps the temporary in scope for the controlled statement. The arrow calls update through the live base-class pointer, choosing the concrete listener function during execution. The compiler checks the shared interface and override signature earlier. Expiration is a normal condition, not an exception. The primary example deliberately destroys one subscriber before publication to show that a registration need not become a dangling raw pointer.

slides.title: Registration rules prevent surprises
keyPoints: subscribe rejects an empty shared pointer, because a null registration has no useful meaning.
The implementation forbids changing the registration list while it is publishing.
slides.narration:
subscribe rejects an empty shared pointer, because a null registration has no useful meaning. It scans existing entries and returns if the same live object is already registered. Subscribing twice therefore produces one update, not two. Expired entries remain in the primary vector but are skipped during publication. This makes the small example simple; a long-lived feed with many short-lived views should periodically remove expired entries so its registration list does not grow forever.

The implementation forbids changing the registration list while it is publishing. subscribe checks notifying_ before doing anything else, even before duplicate detection. This policy protects iteration from vector changes and makes callback behavior predictable. The lab adds unsubscribe with the same rule. A different design could queue registration changes or publish through a stable snapshot of registrations, but then it must state whether a removed listener receives the current event. There is no universal answer that all observers share.

slides.title: Reentrancy is a second call before the first has finished
keyPoints: A callback can call back into its publisher.
The notifying_ flag is set only after input validation and the reentrancy guard.
slides.narration:
A callback can call back into its publisher. If a listener tries feed.publish(1) while handling an earlier publication, the second call is reentrant: the first publish has not returned. Unrestricted recursion can create surprising order, repeated updates, or unbounded calls. This feed rejects nested publish with logic_error. A listener may catch that error and continue, as the primary test does, or allow it to propagate. The behavior is chosen deliberately instead of being an accidental consequence of recursive calls.

The notifying_ flag is set only after input validation and the reentrancy guard. A local Reset object borrows that flag and clears it in its destructor. Its destructor runs on normal return and while an exception unwinds the stack. This is resource acquisition is initialization applied to temporary state, not only memory: the local object owns the duty to reset the flag. Without it, a throwing listener could leave notifying_ true and make every later publication look nested even though the old call had already ended.

slides.title: Failure during delivery is not an all-or-nothing update
keyPoints: Total first adds the reading to sum and then invokes an optional after callback.
This policy is called fail-fast delivery: stop when a callback fails.
slides.narration:
Total first adds the reading to sum and then invokes an optional after callback. In the failure test, adding two changes the total from seven to nine, then after throws. Feed does not catch and continue to later listeners; it propagates the exception and stops the current delivery. Earlier listeners and the throwing listener may already have changed their own state. The Reset destructor clears the flag, so a later publication can run. The next reading of one makes the tested total ten.

This policy is called fail-fast delivery: stop when a callback fails. It is not atomic delivery, in which every listener either receives the change or no listener does. The latter would need much stronger coordination and often cannot be promised for arbitrary outside code. An alternative feed might collect callback errors and continue notifying other listeners. That favors availability but changes error reporting and ordering. In either case, identify whether the feed stores a new reading before publishing and how subscribers recover missed updates. The sample passes event values and keeps no authoritative reading history.

slides.title: Keep callback captures inside a known lifetime
keyPoints: Total exposes a std::function<void()> named after solely as a test hook.
The example is single-threaded.
slides.narration:
Total exposes a std::function<void()> named after solely as a test hook. The empty wrapper means no extra action. The lambda written [&] borrows local objects, including the feed, from main. Those locals remain alive whenever the callback is invoked in this program. Feed itself must stay alive through every active publish call; locking a listener does not keep the publisher alive. Feed deletes copying and assignment and has no implicit move operation, so a callback cannot replace its registration storage by assigning another Feed. Capturing a shared pointer by value inside an object it owns could instead create an ownership cycle. Capturing a short-lived local by reference and invoking it later would leave a dangling reference. A callback is executable state, so its captures deserve the same ownership review as normal members.

The example is single-threaded. weak_ptr provides lifetime coordination for managed objects, but the listener vector, notifying_ flag, and Total::sum are not protected for concurrent access. The total uses int for a small bounded demonstration sequence; an unbounded real stream would require an overflow policy or a wider checked total. Use the pattern to separate interest from production, then write precise rules for delivery, registration, expiration, failure, and concurrency. A diagram with one arrow to each listener is not a substitute for those contracts.

question.answer: No. It manages lifetime, not unsynchronized access to the registration vector and flag. This example does not provide a multithreaded publication contract.

slides.title: Registration observes; a temporary owner protects the call
keyPoints: Feed stores weak_ptr registrations
The client retains shared_ptr ownership
lock obtains a temporary owner only if the listener lives
slides.narration: A weak pointer records a relationship to an object managed by shared ownership without keeping that object alive. Feed therefore does not force a closed view to survive merely because it once subscribed. Before calling update, publish invokes lock on the weak registration. If an owner still exists, lock returns a shared pointer that keeps the listener alive through this callback. If the object has expired, it returns an empty pointer and the feed skips the entry. The if statement both creates live and tests it; live remains in scope inside the branch. This protects the listener during its call. It does not keep Feed itself alive or make arbitrary captured references safe.
actions: Trace the strong owner in main, the weak registration, and the temporary live owner.

question.prompt: Why is checking expiration and then calling a separate raw pointer weaker than using the shared pointer returned by lock?
question.answer: The temporary shared pointer provides ownership through the call. A separate raw pointer does not itself establish that lifetime guarantee.

slides.title: Compile the interface; select the listener at runtime
keyPoints: Listener declares virtual update(int)
Total supplies update with override
Duplicate suppression compares live object identity
slides.narration: Listener defines the one operation Feed needs. virtual allows update to select the concrete implementation during execution, even though Feed holds a pointer through the Listener interface. Total uses override so the compiler checks the signature matches the intended base operation. Those build-time checks do not prove that each listener receives exactly one update. That guarantee also needs registration logic: subscribe rejects an empty pointer and returns when the same live object is already registered. Two distinct Total objects are two listeners even if their sums happen to match. Identity means which object it is, not whether its current fields contain equal values.
actions: Distinguish identity equality from equal display state.

question.prompt: Are two separate Total objects with sum zero duplicate listeners?
question.answer: No. They are distinct object identities and should each receive an event if both are registered and alive.

slides.title: Reject list mutation before touching the list
keyPoints: No subscribe or unsubscribe during publish
The guard runs even for a would-be duplicate
Expired entries are skipped and may be cleaned later
slides.narration: The callback is arbitrary user code, so it might try to change subscriptions. The chapter chooses a simple rule: reject that operation while publishing. subscribe checks notifying_ before duplicate detection, which means subscribing the current listener again is still rejected during its callback. The extension gives unsubscribe the same rule. This keeps vector traversal stable and avoids a question about whether a newly added listener receives the current event. A snapshot-based dispatcher can allow other policies, but it has different lifetime and event-membership costs. Expired entries in the primary program are simply skipped. A long-running feed needs a cleanup plan so dead registrations do not accumulate forever.
actions: Contrast the chapter Feed policy with a clearly labeled snapshot-delivery alternative.

question.prompt: Why is subscribe(existing_listener) rejected inside a callback even though it might not add anything?
question.answer: The contract rejects subscription operations during notification before duplicate detection. It keeps callback mutation behavior uniform and explicit.

slides.title: A destructor can own the duty to clear a flag
keyPoints: A nested publish enters before the first returns
Feed rejects nested publication
Reset clears notifying_ on normal and exceptional exits
slides.narration: Reentrancy means entering publish again while an earlier publish is still active. A callback can do that on the same thread; no second thread is needed. The chapter rejects the nested call to keep event order simple. Once valid publication starts, a local Reset object borrows the busy flag. Its destructor clears that flag when the scope exits, including while an exception unwinds the call stack. This is resource acquisition is initialization used for a cleanup duty rather than heap memory. Clearing the flag only at the last line would fail if a callback threw before reaching it. The guard restores the ability to publish later; it does not roll back listeners' earlier effects.
actions: Trace a callback exception through the Reset destructor to the caller.

question.prompt: Does resetting notifying_ undo the addition made by a throwing Total?
question.answer: No. It restores the feed’s temporary execution state, not the subscriber’s data.

slides.title: Callback captures carry lifetime promises too
keyPoints: [&] captures needed local state by reference
Stored callbacks must not outlive what they borrow
weak_ptr does not synchronize sums or subscription storage
slides.narration: The test hook after is a stored callable. Its lambda capture written with an ampersand borrows the local objects used inside the body. That is safe in the chapter because those objects remain alive whenever the hook is called. Retaining the same hook after a borrowed local died would break a different lifetime rule than the listener registration rule. Capturing a shared pointer can keep an object alive, but storing that callback inside the same owned object can create a cycle. Also separate lifetime from concurrency: a successful weak lock does not lock Total::sum, the vector, or the busy flag. The sample is single-threaded and has no promise of concurrent delivery safety.
actions: Ask learners to list every object borrowed by the chapter’s test callback.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch18.json → Keep callback captures inside a known lifetime

question.prompt: What does a successful weak lock prove, and what does it not prove?
question.answer: It keeps that managed listener alive while the returned shared pointer exists. It does not synchronize mutable state or validate unrelated callback captures.

keyPoints: Publisher / Subject → Feed

A callback throws, and notifying_ is cleared only at the normal end of publish. What defect follows?

Every later notification is guaranteed successful. The flag itself now blocks valid calls.

The callback is automatically removed from all owners. An exception does not imply deregistration.

Earlier observer effects automatically roll back. Observer supplies no such transaction guarantee.

Later publications may all be rejected as nested.. The stale flag survives the exceptional exit; a scope guard must restore it.

question.prompt: Explain Observer without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Feed keeps weak registrations and locks each one for the duration of its call. A scope guard clears the in-progress flag on all exits. Callback errors stop delivery and propagate without claiming rollback. Borrowed raw pointers can be lean when a strict external lifetime and unsubscribe protocol is enforced. A snapshot of strong pointers simplifies stable delivery but keeps listeners alive for the whole batch and changes removal semantics.

slides.title: Choose delivery policy for the application
keyPoints: Fail-fast exposes the first error immediately
Continue-and-collect can keep independent views current
Atomic delivery needs more than Observer
slides.narration: For dependent listeners, stopping after the first failure may be the clearest policy. For independent dashboard views, continuing and collecting errors may keep more of the screen current. Both require tests that include a throwing listener followed by a healthy listener, because normal-path totals cannot distinguish them. Atomic delivery is stronger: either every effect happens or none do. Arbitrary callbacks do not provide a shared rollback mechanism, so Observer alone cannot honestly make that promise. Likewise, weak registrations are one ownership choice, not the pattern's definition. Raw borrowed pointers can work with a strict external lifetime and removal protocol, while strong registrations intentionally retain their listeners.

question.prompt: What single test distinguishes fail-fast from continue-and-collect delivery?
question.answer: Register a throwing listener before a healthy one and publish once. The later listener is skipped by fail-fast and called by continue-and-collect.

slides.title: Test the difficult exit, then the next entry
keyPoints: Failure after a partial update must remain visible
The busy flag must clear after failure
The next ordinary publish must work
slides.narration: A good regression test does not stop after confirming that a callback exception was caught. It clears the throwing hook and publishes again. In the chapter, the total becomes nine before the callback fails, then ten after a later reading of one. If the later call reports nested publish, cleanup was skipped and the busy flag stayed true. If the total returns to seven, someone added rollback behavior that the contract did not define. If a listener receives two updates after duplicate registration, inspect identity suppression. These checks make the event system's promises visible. They also separate delivery recovery from state recovery: the feed may resume even though a prior event reached only part of its audience.

question.prompt: Why test another publish after the throwing callback?
question.answer: It proves the cleanup guard restored the feed’s temporary busy state; merely catching the original exception does not show that.

slides.title: Remember Observer as a relationship plus a contract
keyPoints: A publisher serves a changing registered audience
A shared update operation hides concrete listener types
Lifetime, order, mutation, and failure rules complete the design
slides.narration: Explain Observer in one small story: an object asks to hear events, the publisher remembers that interest, and future events call the listener through a shared update operation. Then add the chapter's exact contract. Live duplicates collapse to one registration, expired listeners are skipped, callbacks run in registration order, subscription changes and nested publish are rejected, and the first thrown error stops delivery without rollback. That second explanation is what lets someone maintain the implementation safely. In a real study application, progress widgets, counters, and alerts may all observe an event. Decide whether a missed update can be recovered from authoritative state or requires replay, because this example keeps no event history for subscribers.

question.prompt: How would you distinguish this Feed from a Mediator?
question.answer: Feed distributes readings to registered listeners. A mediator decides a collaboration policy among components; a listener could use delivered events to perform that coordinating role.
